transcript:
Fireflies.ai Meeting Transcript

Title: TP stability deep dive (multi-GPU) + POC plan
Date: Feb 20, 2025
Time: 9:02 AM PT
Duration: 62 minutes

Attendees:
- Henry Cho (Redwood) 
- Noah Patel (Redwood)
- Hiro Tanaka (Redwood)
- Rafael Mendes (Redwood)
- Priya Nair (HelioBank)
- Evan Liu (HelioBank)
- Marta Kovacs (HelioBank)
- Jordan Wells (HelioBank)

---
Auto Summary (generated)
- HelioBank is evaluating tensor-parallel (TP) inference for larger open models with strict latency SLOs and observed “stuck streams” / timeouts in their current setup.
- Redwood reviewed known failure modes behind TP hangs (collective async errors not surfacing, scheduler barrier/cancellation deadlocks under streaming disconnects, and lack of TP-group health isolation).
- Redwood described mitigations landing in runtime 1.19: async error checks/timeouts, cancellation-safe barriers, and a per-TP-group watchdog that quarantines unhealthy groups.
- Agreed on a controlled POC: start with Dedicated capacity, run a stress suite (mixed seq lengths + long streams + cancellation), and validate watchdog behavior doesn’t cause false positives.

Topics
1) HelioBank workload + current issues
2) Root causes behind TP hangs (comm stall vs kernel stall vs scheduler starvation)
3) Redwood mitigation plan (watchdog/quarantine, error propagation, cancellation semantics)
4) Observability during POC (metrics, dashboards, logs)
5) Deployment mode + rollout plan (Hosted vs Dedicated) and next steps

Questions (captured)
- What does Redwood do when one rank is slow or “wedged”? Does it restart the whole host, or isolate the TP group?
- Can Redwood detect NCCL async errors without waiting for the next blocking call?
- How do you avoid false positives (watchdog firing on legitimately long sequences)?
- If the client disconnects mid-stream, can that deadlock a TP barrier today?
- What’s the timeline for a patch/hotfix and can we run it only for our pool?

---
Transcript

[00:00] Henry Cho: Alright. I think we’re at the top. Thanks everyone for joining. This is, uh, the deep dive on multi-GPU tensor parallel stability. We pulled Noah, who’s our runtime architect, Hiro on kernels and collectives, and Rafael from SRE to talk about guardrails.

[00:17] Priya Nair: Great, thanks Henry. We’ve got Evan, Marta, and Jordan. Jordan is mostly listening for, you know, commercial implications, but we want to focus on the technical risk.

[00:26] Henry Cho: Perfect. Before we jump in, could you give us the 2-minute version of what you’re seeing today? Like symptoms, frequency, impact.

[00:35] Evan Liu: Yeah. So we’ve got… we run, mostly self-hosted right now. For the bigger model, we run 8 GPU TP. And under load, like sustained, we start seeing streaming responses that just, like, stop. Client’s connected, tokens stop. Eventually our gateway times out at 60 seconds, and then we see a spike in 5xx.

[00:56] Evan Liu: And when we look at the GPU boxes, it’s weird: GPU utilization drops on like two ranks, and the others are kind of stuck. No OOM. It’s like a hang. Sometimes it clears if we kill the process; sometimes we have to recycle the node.

[01:13] Marta Kovacs: And from SRE side, the worst part is it doesn’t always crash. It just wedges and keeps accepting traffic until the pool is basically toast.

[01:23] Rafael Mendes: Yep, that’s exactly the failure pattern we’ve been addressing internally. The “stuck but alive” thing is much harder than a clean crash.

[01:31] Henry Cho: Got it. And is this tied to long generations, or just general concurrency?

[01:36] Evan Liu: Both. It’s more frequent when we have long streams, like 2k, 3k tokens output, plus shorter requests mixed in.

[01:45] Priya Nair: We also see it more when clients disconnect. Like mobile clients, flaky networks. We do server-side cancel on disconnect.

[01:54] Noah Patel: That’s a key detail. Cancellation during TP is where a lot of the barrier deadlock issues can appear if the runtime isn’t careful.

[02:03] Henry Cho: Okay. Let’s do this: Noah can frame how our TP execution is structured, then Hiro can talk about collectives and NCCL error propagation, and Rafael can cover watchdog/quarantine and how we operate it. Sound good?

[02:15] Priya Nair: Works.

[02:18] Noah Patel: Alright. So, conceptually, in our runtime each TP group is a failure domain. It’s a fixed set of ranks that together serve a request. The scheduler assigns requests to a TP group, and then within that group we do the forward pass, which includes collective ops—mostly all-reduce / all-gather depending on the architecture.

[02:39] Noah Patel: The hang class we’ve been chasing has three buckets: (1) comm stalls: NCCL collective doesn’t make progress or an async error happened but isn’t surfaced, (2) kernel stalls: a GPU kernel is stuck, often due to cross-stream event ordering, and (3) scheduler starvation / deadlock: the group is waiting at a barrier because one rank took a different path due to cancellation or early-exit.

[03:03] Marta Kovacs: When you say barrier, you mean like “everyone must reach this point before proceeding”?

[03:07] Noah Patel: Exactly. Sometimes it’s explicit, sometimes it’s implicit via collectives. If rank 3 stops participating and rank 0 is blocking in an all-reduce, it’s basically a barrier with teeth.

[03:19] Evan Liu: That sounds like what we see. One rank lags, then the others freeze.

[03:24] Noah Patel: Right. So the plan we’ve executed—some is already in flight—is: make cancellation semantics uniform (so all ranks observe cancel and exit in a coordinated way), improve async error checks for collectives, and add a per-group health model so the scheduler stops routing work to a suspect group.

[03:43] Henry Cho: I’ll pause there. Hiro, can you speak to the NCCL part? They asked specifically about async errors.

[03:50] Hiro Tanaka: Sure. So NCCL and CUDA in general, you can get into this situation where an error occurs on the comm stream, but you don’t get it until a later synchronization point. In practice, if you never hit the right sync or you’re on the wrong stream, you can “spin” and look hung.

[04:07] Hiro Tanaka: What we’re doing in the runtime 1.19 line is periodic async error polling. We check communicator state and CUDA stream status at safe points. We also put a time bound around collectives: if a collective exceeds a threshold, we treat that as a failure and propagate it to the scheduler.

[04:27] Priya Nair: When you say threshold, is it fixed? Because our sequences can be long, and we’ve got… you know, sometimes big batch.

[04:34] Hiro Tanaka: It’s configurable. We’re recommending defaults based on deployment mode. For example, Hosted pools, we’d rather quarantine quickly to protect overall SLA. For Dedicated, you can be a bit more tolerant if you prefer fewer resets.

[04:49] Evan Liu: Quarantine meaning you stop sending traffic to that TP group?

[04:52] Rafael Mendes: Exactly. Let me explain how we operate it. If a TP group stops making forward progress—meaning tokens aren’t being emitted and internal progress counters aren’t moving—we mark it unhealthy. The scheduler stops assigning new requests to it, drains what it can, and then does a controlled teardown.

[05:11] Marta Kovacs: Does it tear down the whole process or just that group?

[05:14] Rafael Mendes: Depends on the packaging. In most of our deployments, one process owns a group, so tearing down the group is effectively restarting that worker process. We try hard not to recycle the node unless necessary.

[05:29] Priya Nair: That’s good. We’ve had vendors that just restart the entire machine and it causes like a 5-minute outage.

[05:35] Noah Patel: Yeah, we’re trying to keep the blast radius to a group. And importantly, we track it as an explicit metric: watchdog triggers, quarantines, resets, and how many requests were impacted.

[05:49] Henry Cho: Maybe we should address the elephant in the room: have you seen this happen on Redwood today? Like in production.

[05:55] Rafael Mendes: We have seen it, yes, primarily in high-load multi-GPU pools. That’s why this project exists. The difference is we’ve now got repro patterns and fixes that are moving through. There was a Sev1 in Feb that accelerated it.

[06:10] Priya Nair: Okay, appreciate the honesty.

[06:12] Henry Cho: The goal here is to make sure you’re comfortable we can support a controlled POC without you becoming our test environment.

[06:21] Evan Liu: Right, that’s basically our worry.

[06:24] Noah Patel: For POC, we’d propose a very instrumented setup: Dedicated capacity, specific runtime build, and a known stress pattern that includes the “mixed lengths + cancellation + sustained streams.” We also tune watchdog sensitivity to avoid false positives.

[06:44] Marta Kovacs: Can you talk about false positives? We’ve tried watchdogs in other systems and it’s like… it just kills workers during normal long requests.

[06:52] Rafael Mendes: Totally. The key is we don’t look at wall clock only. We look at per-rank progress. For example, has the decode loop advanced? Are collectives completing? Are we seeing heartbeats from each rank? A legitimately long request still shows progress. A wedged group shows flat lines.

[07:14] Priya Nair: What about slowdowns? Like one rank is slower due to thermal or noisy neighbor.

[07:20] Rafael Mendes: Then you’d see progress but degraded. We treat that as “slow,” not “stuck.” Alerts are different. We can also add backpressure so that group doesn’t get the hardest work.

[07:32] Noah Patel: This touches scheduling fairness. Mixed seq lengths can cause head-of-line blocking if you’re not careful with continuous batching. We’ve made changes so long-running streams don’t monopolize a group.

[07:46] Evan Liu: When you say changes, are they shipped?

[07:50] Noah Patel: Some are in the 1.19 branch. Some are behind flags in current builds. We’ll be clear which ones we’re proposing for your POC.

[08:00] Henry Cho: Evan, Marta—do you know your GPU type and driver versions? Just so we’re comparing apples.

[08:06] Evan Liu: For our lab it’s A100 80GB, driver is… I wanna say 535? CUDA 12.2 maybe. Production we’re moving to H100 but not there yet.

[08:19] Hiro Tanaka: Okay. We’ve seen some differences across driver lines, but the failure modes you’re describing are not only driver related.

[08:28] Priya Nair: You mentioned cancellation. Can you explain what specifically can deadlock?

[08:33] Noah Patel: Yeah. Simplifying a bit: if a client disconnects and rank 0 sees cancellation first, it might try to exit early. But rank 1-7 may still be mid-step and expecting a collective. If rank 0 stops participating in a collective that others are in, you get a hang.

[08:54] Noah Patel: The fix is to make cancel a coordinated state: once any rank sees it, we broadcast the cancel intent to all ranks in the group, and we exit at a safe boundary where everyone agrees. No one “peels off” mid-collective.

[09:12] Evan Liu: That matches what we suspected. We found logs like “client disconnect” right before the hang.

[09:18] Marta Kovacs: But then the request is “canceled” and the worker is still busy for 60 seconds. That’s a different type of failure.

[09:26] Noah Patel: Right. Cancellation has to be prompt but also correct. We prefer “cancel at a safe point” rather than “cancel instantly and deadlock.” With proper instrumentation, we can see where the delay is.

[09:40] Henry Cho: Let’s talk observability. Marta, what do you need for your oncall to feel comfortable during POC?

[09:46] Marta Kovacs: We need to know: is it comm stall, is it kernel stall, is it scheduler starvation. And what do we do? Shift traffic? Restart worker? Increase timeout? Right now it’s too opaque.

[09:59] Rafael Mendes: For POC we can give you a set of dashboards: collective latency histograms, per-rank progress counters, and watchdog triggers. Also structured logs that say “collective stalled > threshold” or “barrier wait exceeded.”

[10:14] Priya Nair: Are those in your console? Or do we need Prometheus.

[10:18] Rafael Mendes: For Dedicated, we support both. If you’re using Redwood Console, you’ll see it. If you want to scrape metrics into your Prometheus, we can do that too.

[10:28] Jordan Wells: Sorry, quick question. In Dedicated, do we get those dashboards included or is it an add-on?

[10:34] Henry Cho: For the POC, we’ll include it. Long term, advanced retention is an add-on, but the core operational metrics are part of the package.

[10:45] Priya Nair: Okay. Now, timeline: we’re planning a POC starting mid-March. Do you expect these fixes to be stable by then?

[10:55] Henry Cho: We’re targeting runtime 1.19 as the stabilization release. Some pieces are already merged; we’re also doing a patch line if needed. For mid-March, we can run you on the 1.19 build with the TP stability flags enabled.

[11:12] Evan Liu: Are these default on?

[11:15] Henry Cho: In Hosted, we’ll turn them on progressively. In Dedicated, we can do opt-in first, then default once we’re confident. That’s also something we want your input on.

[11:28] Priya Nair: We’d prefer opt-in with very clear rollback.

[11:31] Rafael Mendes: That’s standard. We define rollback triggers: watchdog trigger rate, reset rate, and of course customer-visible error rate/latency.

[11:42] Hiro Tanaka: And we watch for performance regression. The goal is no heavy synchronization. The error checks are designed to be low overhead.

[11:51] Evan Liu: Can you quantify overhead? Like 1%, 5%?

[11:55] Hiro Tanaka: Early measurements show under 1% for typical decode workloads. But it depends on how aggressive the polling is. That’s why we provide a knob.

[12:07] Noah Patel: Another point: the watchdog isn’t running in the hot path every token. It’s periodic sampling plus counters that already exist.

[12:16] Priya Nair: Good.

[12:18] Henry Cho: Can I ask what model you’re targeting? If you can share.

[12:22] Priya Nair: We’re evaluating a couple open models in the 70B class. Possibly 100B-ish later. Right now we need 70B with decent latency.

[12:33] Evan Liu: And we have strict p95. For chat, under 1.5 seconds time-to-first-token, and then stable throughput.

[12:42] Noah Patel: Understood. For 70B on 8x H100, you can hit that with the right batching. The stability work is to ensure you don’t get tail disasters.

[12:54] Marta Kovacs: On failure domains—if one TP group is quarantined, do you have enough capacity to absorb? Or do you start dropping traffic.

[13:03] Rafael Mendes: In Dedicated, we’d size with headroom. For POC, we can also test “single group down” scenarios. The scheduler will route to remaining healthy groups, and if you’re saturated, you’ll see backpressure rather than indefinite hanging.

[13:20] Evan Liu: Backpressure meaning 429 or queueing.

[13:23] Noah Patel: Depends on your config: queue with max wait, or shed load. The key is deterministic behavior.

[13:31] Priya Nair: I like that. Our main pain is nondeterministic stalls.

[13:36] Henry Cho: Any security concerns for Dedicated POC? Data handling, logs, etc.

[13:42] Priya Nair: We’ll likely need audit logs and encryption. But for POC, we can use synthetic prompts. No PII.

[13:50] Jordan Wells: And we’ll need a basic SOC2 package, but later.

[13:55] Henry Cho: Got it. We can send standard security docs under NDA. For now, we’ll keep prompts synthetic.

[14:05] Evan Liu: Back to the hang: do you have a way to tell comm stall vs kernel stall automatically?

[14:12] Hiro Tanaka: We can infer. If collectives are taking abnormally long and GPU kernels around them are finishing, it points to comm. If you see a kernel never completes on a stream, it’s more kernel stall. We also add log markers around collective begin/end.

[14:31] Noah Patel: Also, scheduler starvation shows up as no kernel launches at all plus a barrier wait metric climbing.

[14:39] Marta Kovacs: And you’ll expose these as metrics?

[14:41] Rafael Mendes: Yes. For POC, we’ll provide a minimal set: tp_group_forward_progress_seconds, collective_latency_ms buckets, watchdog_trigger_total, tp_group_quarantine_total, and reset reason labels.

[15:00] Priya Nair: Nice.

[15:02] Henry Cho: I’m going to jump to the POC structure so we can align. Proposal: two-week POC on Dedicated. Week 1: baseline throughput/latency and run stress suite with no fault injection. Week 2: introduce cancellation storms and rank delay injection to validate the watchdog and recovery.

[15:22] Evan Liu: Rank delay injection—how do you do that.

[15:25] Noah Patel: We have a test harness that can deliberately sleep one rank at specific steps, or inject artificial GPU sync points. It’s not perfect, but it reproduces the “lagging rank” behavior.

[15:38] Priya Nair: That’s exactly what we want. Because in the real world we’ll have occasional slowdowns.

[15:44] Marta Kovacs: But if you inject it, does it cause false positives. That’s the test.

[15:48] Rafael Mendes: Right. We can tune thresholds and see. We also validate we don’t cascade into repeated resets.

[15:58] Jordan Wells: Sorry, are we talking about a custom build for POC?

[16:02] Henry Cho: Not “custom” in the sense of one-off. It’s our upcoming stable runtime version. But yes, we may run you on a canary build with some flags enabled.

[16:12] Priya Nair: Okay. Can we get clarity on what changes are actually in the build?

[16:17] Hiro Tanaka: We’ll send a list. The big ones: periodic async error checks, collective timeout handling, and improved failure propagation into the scheduler. Also some safer stream/event ordering in a couple kernels.

[16:34] Noah Patel: And on scheduling: cancellation-safe barrier coordination and tp-group state machine so quarantined groups don’t receive new work.

[16:45] Evan Liu: That last one is huge. Our current system keeps sending traffic to the wedged worker.

[16:50] Rafael Mendes: Exactly. That’s why it becomes a pool-wide incident.

[16:55] Priya Nair: What about recovery? When you quarantine and reset, do you lose the in-flight requests.

[17:02] Noah Patel: Yes, those in-flight requests will fail. We try to fail fast with a clear error. For some workloads, we can re-route if the request is idempotent, but for streaming generation, typically it’s an error and the client retries.

[17:18] Priya Nair: That’s acceptable if it’s rare and bounded.

[17:22] Marta Kovacs: We’d rather have a clean failure than a 60-second hang.

[17:27] Henry Cho: That’s our philosophy too.

[17:31] Evan Liu: Do you support “graceful fallback” to a smaller model when capacity is constrained or group is down?

[17:37] Henry Cho: In Hosted we have policy-based fallback. In Dedicated, we can do routing across model variants if you deploy both, but it’s usually a deliberate configuration.

[17:49] Priya Nair: For POC we probably keep it simple: one model.

[17:53] Henry Cho: Agreed.

[18:00] (cross talk)

[18:02] Marta Kovacs: One more: we saw NCCL errors sometimes but not always. Like “unhandled system error” and then everything is stuck.

[18:10] Hiro Tanaka: Yeah. That’s the async error propagation problem. Sometimes the first rank hits it, others don’t. If you don’t poll and propagate, you get a partial failure and deadlock.

[18:24] Evan Liu: That’s exactly it.

[18:27] Noah Patel: In our approach, if any rank reports a comm error, we mark the whole group unhealthy and abort the group. It’s harsh but correct.

[18:37] Priya Nair: Does aborting risk corrupting GPU state.

[18:41] Hiro Tanaka: There’s always risk, but controlled teardown is safer than letting it hang forever. We also isolate per-group resources as much as possible.

[18:53] Rafael Mendes: Operationally, we also cap retries. If a host starts resetting repeatedly, we mark the host out of rotation.

[19:03] Marta Kovacs: Great. That’s like circuit breaker.

[19:06] Rafael Mendes: Exactly.

[19:10] Henry Cho: We’re at about 20 minutes. I want to make sure we cover the questions you brought. Priya, anything we haven’t answered yet?

[19:17] Priya Nair: Two things. One: can you run this in our VPC. Two: can we get an SLO or SLA commitment on TP stability.

[19:26] Henry Cho: For VPC, yes, that’s our Private / VPC deployment option. For the POC you were leaning Dedicated, which is isolated capacity in our cloud. If you need VPC from day one, we can discuss.

[19:39] Priya Nair: For now Dedicated is okay. We’ll likely need VPC later.

[19:44] Henry Cho: On SLO/SLA: for POC we typically define success criteria rather than contractual SLA. Post-POC, Dedicated contracts include uptime SLOs. For TP-specific, we can commit to error rate and latency targets, but we’ll want to align on definitions.

[20:05] Rafael Mendes: And internally, for this initiative, we’re tracking reductions in timeouts/5xx and watchdog trigger rates. We can share those metrics during POC.

[20:17] Priya Nair: Good.

[20:19] Evan Liu: Can you share logs examples of what we’ll see when a stall happens? Like the “signature.”

[20:26] Noah Patel: We can share sanitized examples. It’ll show “collective op took X ms exceeding threshold” and the group id, rank, and the last known progress step.

[20:39] Hiro Tanaka: And sometimes the transcription—sorry, the log text—might mention “NCLL” because someone spelled it wrong. (laughs)

[20:45] Henry Cho: Noted.

[20:48] Priya Nair: Okay.

[20:50] Henry Cho: I think we’re aligned. Let’s do a quick round of next steps and owners.

[20:55] Henry Cho: I’ll send a concise write-up of the mitigation plan and the 1.19 timeline, plus a proposed POC outline.

[21:03] Noah Patel: I’ll send recommended knobs: collective timeout, watchdog sensitivity, and cancellation behavior. Also what metrics to collect.

[21:10] Hiro Tanaka: I’ll confirm which fixes are in the hotfix branch versus mainline and any known caveats.

[21:16] Rafael Mendes: I’ll share the alerting/operational guardrails we use, like trigger thresholds and rollback criteria.

[21:24] Marta Kovacs: I’ll send our environment details: GPU type, driver, CUDA, and our current timeouts and cancellation settings.

[21:33] Evan Liu: And I’ll send an example of the traffic shape: concurrency, output tokens, and the “disconnect rate.”

[21:40] Priya Nair: Then we schedule the POC scoping call.

[21:44] Henry Cho: Great. Anything else before we wrap?

[21:48] Jordan Wells: No, thank you. This was helpful.

[21:51] Priya Nair: Thanks everyone.

[21:53] Henry Cho: Thanks all. We’ll follow up by tomorrow with the docs.

(Transcript ended early in export; remaining time likely Q&A off-record / dropped audio.)
